_about: The Character creator: a character made outside any film, from a description (and a reference picture), in one drawing style, by one Claude Code run in a lab folder outside git (<work>/library/characters/_lab/<job>/), then saved to the user's library. Styles: the 9 hands of anidoodle's human engine (Alex Greenshpun, Apache-2.0, pinned in config/pins.json anidoodle; the author's recipe) and Brush cartoon (ClaudeAnimationBase's kit, John Heibel, MIT; the app's character layer). The prompts are templates: {{DESCRIPTION}}, {{ID}}, {{NAME}}, {{HAND}}, {{HAND_LABEL}}, {{REFERENCE}} (a line about the picture, or nothing), {{CHANGE}} (the change asked, for Change with Claude, or nothing). The estimates are measured (two human characters, 34 and 38 minutes, $6.76 and $11.21 at API prices).

styles.label: Storybook (pencil + watercolour)
styles.example: the author's own hand for Mira's approved sheet

styles.label: Marker comic (flat cels, one heavy line)
styles.example: the closest to a flat 2D motion look

rigs._about: What the character is: chosen before the hand. Each engine offers the kinds it can draw; the kind picks the recipe and the gate: a person on anidoodle's human engine is checked by the author's human rules; an animal or a thing gets a rig of its own and a gate of its own rules, never the human limits (as with a turtle, commit 0437ba4a). Brush cartoon's layer draws mascots, so it offers an animal or a thing, not a person.

human.label: Human
human.about: A person, on anidoodle's human engine: the author's recipe and the author's human gate.

animal.label: Animal
animal.about: An animal: a rig of its own (its own bones and limits) and a gate of its own rules.

thing.label: Thing
thing.about: An object or a creature that is neither (a lamp, a cloud, a cube of tofu): a rig of its own and a gate of its own rules.

robot.label: Robot
robot.about: A robot or a machine with a body (as the author's Bit): a rig of its own and a gate of its own rules, never the human limits.

anidoodle-human.measured: audit 63 §12: 33.6 min / $6.76 and 37.9 min / $11.21 (API prices; on a Claude plan it counts against the plan's usage)

brush-kit.measured: audit 63 §13: Mochi, 1.9 min / $0.38 at API prices, 15 turns, two sheet rounds; a showreel adds about a minute

prompts.anidoodle-human:
You are building ONE character for Moworks Studio's character library, the way anidoodle's author builds a character: on the author's human engine, as shipped, kept as a module that films will pose later.

The character: {{DESCRIPTION}}
Its id (folder and export names): {{ID}}. Its name: {{NAME}}.
Its drawing style (anidoodle's hand): {{HAND_LABEL}} (`{{HAND}}`).
{{REFERENCE}}{{CHANGE}}
## What you have

- The anidoodle engine, pinned and staged as shipped, in `.moworks/library/anidoodle/` (read it; never edit anything under `.moworks/`). Import it in your code as `anidoodle/...`, e.g. `anidoodle/canvas-core/character/human/figure`.
- The author's recipe for a new character: `.moworks/library/anidoodle/references/workflows/character-consistency.md`, `references/anatomy.md`, `references/craft-bar.md`. Follow it.
- The worked examples: Mira (`engine/src/canvas-core/characters/mira/`: index.ts, drawn.ts, poses.ts, palettes.ts), Theo (`characters/theo/`, wardrobe.ts for garments), the human engine (`character/human/`: canon, skeleton, mannequin, head with EXPRESSIONS, hands, clothing, figure, walk, balance), the 2.5D drawn parts (`character/view25d.ts`), the hand that draws a Scene in this style (`engine/src/canvas-core/{{RENDER}}.ts`; Mira's palette for it in `characters/mira/palettes.ts`, how her tile calls it in `miraTile.ts`), Mira's model sheet (`miraSheet.ts`) and walk (`miraWalk.ts`). Study them; do not copy Mira.
- The author's own gate for Mira and Theo, as a reference: `reference/character-check.entry.ts` (its checks live in `character/check.ts`).
- Three commands (run them from this folder; nothing else is available):
  - `node tools/gate.mjs check.ts` runs your gate (`anidoodle/check.ts`), prints PASS/FAIL per check, exits 1 on a failure.
  - `node tools/still.mjs films/<file>.ts out/<file>.png` renders frame 0 of a film module to a PNG you can then look at with Read.
  - `node tools/render.mjs films/<file>.ts out/<file>.mp4` renders a whole film (slow: only if you must; the app renders the final walk after you).
  A film module mounts its film and exports its meta: `import { mountFilm } from "anidoodle/hosts/page"; mountFilm(film); export const __meta = film.meta;`.

## What to make (all under `anidoodle/`)

1. `characters/{{ID}}/`: the character module, the author's contract (types.ts): canon row (declare a stylised or age row if this body needs one), spec, rig, drawn 2.5D parts where a volume cannot describe a feature, palette ROLES, distinguishing FEATURES with the views they must appear in, `toScene(pose, camera)`, a pose library (relaxed, wave, and two poses that suit this person) validated against the joint limits, and the palette for the `{{HAND}}` hand. Export `{{ID}}` (the Character), and its SPEC, FEATURES, ROLES and poses.
2. `films/sheet.ts`: the model sheet in the `{{HAND}}` hand, one frame: turnaround (front, three-quarter, profile, back), the six expressions (neutral, happy, laughing, surprised, worried, determined), the poses, labelled.
3. `films/walk.ts`: a 3 s walk (1920 x 1080, 30 fps, 90 frames) in the `{{HAND}}` hand, the walk from footsteps (`planWalk` / `walkAt`), the author's way, on a simple ground that suits the hand.
4. `check.ts`: the character gate, exporting `run()` like the reference: canon, every library pose inside the joint limits and balanced, hands, identity per view (every feature in the views it should be), palette roles in family for this hand (and lightness for whites, greys and blacks, which a hue check cannot hold), and the walk's planted feet; plus NEGATIVE TWINS that must fail.
5. `LEDGER.md`: one line per round: what the gate or your look at the sheet found wrong, and what you changed.
6. `character.json`: `{ "id": "{{ID}}", "name": "<its name>", "about": "<one sentence: who, the features a child would remember>", "heightM": <its real height in metres, to the top of the head (an animal standing; a thing or a robot at its tallest)>, "heightBy": "description" when the description names it, else "inferred" (a real-world size for what it is), "heightNote": "<a few words: what the number measures>" }`. A person's heightM is the height in its spec (the one its rig and gates use).

## How

Build it, run the gate, render the sheet and LOOK at it against the description and the reference picture (the distinguishing features, the silhouette, the age and build). Fix what is wrong and go again. Stop when the gate passes and the sheet reads as this person; at most 6 rounds. Nobody answers questions here: where the description leaves something open (age, build, clothes), choose what fits it and go on. Finish with a short summary in the language of the description above (the owner reads it): what was hard, what still looks wrong, and which features the engine could not draw well. Write only under `anidoodle/` and `out/`.
prompts.brush-kit:
You are making ONE character for Moworks Studio's character library, for the Brush cartoon style: a mascot drawn by the app's character layer on ClaudeAnimationBase's kit, outside any film.

The character: {{DESCRIPTION}}
Its id: {{ID}}. Its name: {{NAME}}.
What it is: {{RIG_LABEL}}. The layer draws it as a mascot (a body with a face, legs and arms): an animal reads by its shape, colours and the features you give it, a thing by its silhouette and what it holds.
{{REFERENCE}}{{CHANGE}}
## What you have

- The rules: `.moworks/rules/brush-cartoon/SKILL.md` (ClaudeAnimationBase's ANIMATION_GUIDE.md as shipped) and `.moworks/rules/brush-cartoon-app/SKILL.md` (how the app draws characters: §3). Clawd is Anthropic's mascot and is never a character here.
- The definition schema: `.moworks/library/character-kit/examples/definition.json` (the fields of a definition, never a character to draw) and the character layer `.moworks/library/character-kit/src/character.js`.
- One command (run it from this folder; nothing else is available): `node tools/brush-sheets.mjs` draws the model sheets of CHARACTERS.json into `characters/sheets/{{ID}}-views.png` (the five views, moves and hats) and `{{ID}}-emotions.png` (all 31 emotions), which you then look at with Read. It then prints each character's gate (PASS / FAIL with the reason: the schema, never Clawd, colours that separate and read on a light and a dark ground, the face on the body, legs under it reaching the ground, arms at its sides, the key views, the sheets not blank); the app saves the character only when every check passes.

## What to make

`CHARACTERS.json` with one definition, `{ "characters": [ { "id": "{{ID}}", ... } ] }` (with `heightM`: its real height in metres at its tallest, `heightBy`: "description" when the description names it, else "inferred", and `heightNote`: a few words on what the number measures; The Studio stands every character on a height chart), simple enough to act and readable at phone size. Draw the sheets, read them once and hold them against the description and the reference picture: every feature named (hair, clothes, a prop or something held, its colours) must show. Add what is missing to the definition, and fix a real problem (a face off the body, a part that does not read at phone size, colours that do not separate from each other or from a light and a dark background), then draw them again, once or twice at most, and until the gate passes. The id stays `{{ID}}`; never `clawd`, and never Clawd's shape or colours. Nobody answers questions here: where the description leaves something open, choose and go on. Write only CHARACTERS.json. Finish, in the language of the description above (the owner reads it), with one short line on what the character is and one line naming any feature the character layer cannot draw (or that every feature is there).

It is never a person: never the human engine's canon, skeleton, mannequin or joint limits, and never the author's human gate.

The character: {{DESCRIPTION}}
